articles.summary: UK News: A baby’s name is often chosen for its meaning, family history or cultural tradition. But for Katie Murphy, 33, and Stephen Kirby, 32, the choice came .
articles.body: A baby’s name is often chosen for its meaning, family history or cultural tradition. But for Katie Murphy, 33, and Stephen Kirby, 32, the choice came down to circumstance and a car park that would define their son’s entire origin story. Katie and her partner welcomed their son in unexpected circumstances, which prompted them to name him after KFC’s famous founder, Colonel Harland Sanders, news agency SWNS reported.Hours after being sent home, woman goes into labour on the A38It was August 29. Katie Murphy and her partner drove to the hospital early in the morning after she felt the baby was coming. The doctors examined her, told her everything was fine and sent her back home. The contractions had started before they left the hospital, intensifying during the thirty-minute drive back to Bromsgrove. “They got more intense when we were at home, but Katie didn’t want to go back to [the] hospital yet in case we were turned away,” Kirby told the outlet.Eight hours later, the contractions grew stronger. The couple had no choice but to head to the hospital again. “Finally, at around 9 p.m., she was in so much discomfort that we just said, ‘Let’s go,’ and I got her in a car to get to the hospital,” he said. “The drive is around half an hour, but around halfway through the journey, Katie said she could feel something and knew the baby was coming,” Kirby said. He was on the phone to get an ambulance. “They were asking what our location was, but we were on the A38, and there was nowhere to pull in.” The A38 traffic hummed around them, with no exits in sight.Giving birth in KFC’s car parkThat’s when Kirby saw the KFC. Not a hospital, not an ambulance station, but a car park with pavement, light and witnesses. He knew this was their salvation. It was the KFC they frequented. He pulled in at 9:35 p.m. “Thankfully, I saw the KFC we often go to and pulled into the car park,” he said.As they pulled into the space, the woman could feel her baby’s head emerging. Kirby raced around to the passenger side, opened the door and caught their newborn before anything else happened. And there he was: a baby boy, born in a car in a fast-food car park. “When the ambulance dispatcher was trying to locate our location, the only place we could find was the KFC. As my partner pulled into the car park, and as he made his way round to the passenger side and opened the door, he caught my son just in time,” the new mum told the agency.They named him Colonel CodyThe baby was in perfect health. The newborn weighed 7 lb, 8 oz. Now was the time to name the baby. They named him Cody. But it came with a nickname: Colonel Cody, after KFC’s Colonel Harland Sanders.“We call him Colonel Cody, and I think that nickname will definitely stick with him for life,” the mother said.The fast-food restaurant chain was undoubtedly glad to hear the family nicknaming the baby after its founder. In a statement, a KFC spokesperson said, “We’re honoured to have been the place of Cody’s birth and are sending bucket loads of love to the whole family, along with some KFC merch and vouchers to help them celebrate. We can’t wait to welcome them back for a meal to mark the occasion.”The new parents are already planning his first birthday trip. Back to the same KFC; a homecoming of sorts. There’s talk of a weekend job when he’s old enough, a joke that might not stay a joke. “We were famous amongst the midwifery staff, and they even ordered KFC for dinner. It was decided that we have to take him to KFC for his first birthday and get him his first weekend job there,” the mum said.Minutes after giving birth, the ambulance arrived and took the family to the hospital. “It all happened so fast. Thankfully, the ambulance was with us about five minutes later and took us to the hospital. Despite his abrupt entrance into the world in his dad’s car, Cody is in perfect health and is doing great,” the new mum recalled. The mother and the newborn got the medical attention they needed. And Cody’s unusual birth is a one-of-a-kind story that is sure to dominate family dinner conversations for years to come. “It was definitely not the birth I expected, but it was worth every bit of pain, and now he has a very weird story to tell his school friends when he grows up,” Katie Murphy said.Catch the latest World News and Live updates. articles.title: In 2007, Scottish cyclist Mark Beaumont left Paris to race around Earth; 194 days and 17 hours later, crashes, theft and exhaustion had not stopped him
articles.summary: UK News: In 2007, Mark Beaumont set off from Paris on a remarkable solo journey, cycling around the globe in just 194 days. Overcoming crashes, theft, and exhaustion, his adventure redefined endurance cycling and raised £18,000 for charity. Read on to explore how he inspired a generation of cyclists!
articles.body: Long before ultra-endurance sport became a global spectacle, crossing the world on two wheels was the domain of the odd and the dreamer. Record keepers had been tracking efforts at this achievement for decades, and the bar kept moving as riders pushed further into the unknown with little more than paper maps, panniers and persistence. A young man from rural Fife, a man who had spent his childhood cycling throughout Scotland for enjoyment, stepped into that bloodline in the summer of 2007. What came next would see him become one of the defining figures in endurance riding and rewrite what people thought was physically feasible on a bicycle.On 5 August 2007, Mark Beaumont left the Arc de Triomphe in Paris on a laden touring bike with an objective that appeared almost reckless for someone who had never attempted anything on this scale before. He planned to ride about 100 miles a day, alone and unsupported, until he had travelled round the globe and got back to where he started. His bicycle, a Koga Miyata with a Rohloff internal gear hub, was loaded with around 30 kilogrammes of tools, spare parts and video equipment, since he was chronicling the voyage himself for what would become a BAFTA nominated BBC film. Cycling UK, the membership club that has long backed British riders on just this sort of personal endeavour, later published his own report of how three years of planning went into that single departure from Paris.A path through hardshipBeaumont’s journey carried him east via Europe and Russia, through Central Asia and the Indian subcontinent, across Southeast Asia and Australia, and then across North America before one more trans-Atlantic trip back to France. It was a tough trail, and preparation wouldn’t make it easier. In Lafayette, Louisiana, he was hit by a car and robbed later that same day, an experience that would have killed most people’s endeavours on the spot. Elsewhere he fought illness and the sort of physical disintegration that comes from sixteen or more hours a day in the saddle for months on end without rest. He’d also meant to be a vegetarian but had little choice but to give that up during the ride simply to keep enough calories going in to survive the daily mileage.It’s not only the distance but also the isolation that makes the achievement exceptional. Throughout the ride, Beaumont had no support car, no mechanic and no chef. If his gear broke or his body let him down, he had to tackle the problem himself, often in isolated parts of Pakistan, Iran or the Australian outback where help was hours or days away. He used paper maps in an age when smartphone navigation didn’t even exist for bikes and had his mother back home assist him in plotting alternative routes if roads were blocked.Rewriting the recordOn 15 February 2008, Beaumont cycled back past the Arc de Triomphe, having completed almost 18,000 miles in 194 days and 17 hours. That broke the previous world record by 81 days, a margin so vast that even veteran endurance athletes who had thought the mark would stand for years were startled. His accomplishment was officially validated, and the lineage of riders who chased and ultimately beat his time is still recorded on the official Guinness World Records page for the quickest circumnavigation by bicycle. Other cyclists would eventually beat Beaumont's own record, such as Vin Cox in 2010, before Beaumont himself recaptured the supported version of the championship in 2017 with a specially organised support squad, further lowering his own original time.But it is the 2007 solo ride that attracted public attention, because he did it without a safety net. Beaumont then returned to his old university, the University of St Andrews, to speak to students about the trip. He didn't frame it as some prank, but as proof that ordinary preparedness, stubbornness and a tolerance for discomfort might take a person further than nearly anyone expected. The ride raised £18,000 for charity and he utilised the platform it established to launch a series of additional expeditions including the length of the Americas trip from Alaska to Argentina and a solo unsupported crossing from Cairo to Cape Town.Nearly two decades later, Beaumont's original circumnavigation is still cited as a moment when unsupported round-the-world cycling moved from an oddity to a recognised branch of endurance sport, inspiring later solo riders like Jenny Graham and a wave of amateur cyclists who attempt similar routes every year. It’s not just the miles that keep the story alive, but what it said about the extremes individuals will reach when curiosity and discipline collide.Catch the latest World News and Live updates. articles.title: In 2016, airborne laser scans around Angkor revealed vast hidden roads, ponds and neighbourhoods, showing the Khmer capital stretched far beyond its famous temples
articles.summary: Rest of World News: In 2016, airborne lidar scans around Angkor revealed hidden roads, canals, ponds and residential areas beneath Cambodia’s forests, showing the Khmer capital was far larger and more complex than its famous temples suggested.
articles.body: For more than a century, most people knew the grand capital of the Khmer Empire by what they saw from above, the vast stone temples of Angkor Wat and surrounding monuments. The common people of Angkor lived and moved along roads lined with houses and everyday structures built of wood and thatch, which rotted away centuries ago and left little for archaeologists to see sticking up out of the ground; thus, the temples never told the story of the huge urban environment that once surrounded them. It took a chopper with a laser on top to finally unveil what had been hiding below the Cambodian jungle canopy all along.University of Sydney archaeologist Damian Evans had spent years collecting pieces of Angkor’s urban footprint via painstaking ground surveys before turning to a form of airborne laser scanning technology known as lidar. The first survey in 2012 scanned 370 square kilometres of the wider Angkor region, using a helicopter-mounted scanner that sent quick laser pulses into the ground, penetrating dense vegetation to record subtle differences in the earth's surface that showed traces of long-vanished roadways, canals and building platforms. Within that scanned area, the survey, published in the Proceedings of the National Academy of Sciences, more than tripled the confirmed footprint of Angkor's densely built city centre, from nine square kilometres of previously documented terrain to 35.A city bigger than anyone could have dreamedThe early successes led Evans and his team to return in 2015 to carry out what became the biggest airborne archaeological survey in history, spanning approximately 1,901 square kilometres of rainforest roughly the size of Greater London. The findings, published in the Journal of Archaeological Science in 2016, demonstrated that Angkor's full urban sprawl, well beyond that initial city-centre core, spread outwards in all directions for about 1,000 square km from its temple centre. Major temples were connected to residential districts beneath the forest canopy by a complicated rectilinear road system, and seasonal flood regions were spanned by raised road beds, with smaller side roads branching out into dwelling sections.Perhaps most startling was discovering thousands of small rectangular lumps uniformly spread over what the scans identified as residential areas, the bases of wooden buildings that had originally been on raised platforms but left no trace either from the ground or from earlier satellite imagery.The survey also showed a vast network of canals, channels and embankments running parallel to the road network, forming a sophisticated system of water management across the landscape, evidence of an urban civilisation engineering its environment on a scale far beyond that suggested by temple architecture alone. The study was funded by the European Research Council, which also backed the technical side of the project and later financed further rounds of Evans's lidar work across Southeast Asian archaeologyA retelling of the tale of a lost capitalThe scans confirmed and extended earlier discoveries about Mahendraparvata, an early Khmer capital first identified in 2012 beneath the Phnom Kulen mountain, and showed it to be considerably larger than initial ground surveys had indicated, covering fifteen to twenty square miles of terrain now completely reclaimed by forest. The wider picture of Angkor's population, which some estimates suggest could have supported anything from 750,000 to a million people, made it comparable in scale to major cities anywhere in the world at the time, the researchers involved in the project said. It was a striking realisation for a civilisation whose visible remains had, for so long, been reduced to a handful of temple complexes.The findings have changed the way that historians understand the rise and eventual destruction of Angkor. Researchers have given a new perspective to theories about the decline of the once mighty capital, suggesting that the later population growth of the empire put unsustainable pressure on its agricultural base. This is because they have a better understanding of how much of the surrounding landscape was used for residential and infrastructural purposes, rather than for rice farming. What began as an attempt to verify patchy evidence on the ground has produced one of the most complete views of a centuries-old Southeast Asian city to date, hidden in plain sight beneath a forest that has kept its secrets for the best part of six centuries.Catch the latest World News and Live updates. articles.title: A sea captain built this Nantucket house around 1834; after being moved and restored twice, the 7,000-plus-square-foot home that sold for $9.5 million is now listed for $32 million
articles.summary: News News: A historic Nantucket home with a past as remarkable as its architecture has returned to the luxury property market with a $32 million price tag. Built.
articles.body: A historic Nantucket home with a past as remarkable as its architecture has returned to the luxury property market with a $32 million price tag. Built around 1834 for sea captain George C. Gardner, the Greek Revival house has survived decades of change, including a move to its current location and two major restoration efforts. The 7,000-plus-square-foot residence at 141 Main Street later sold for $9.5 million after its most recent restoration. Now, the George C. Gardner House combines its 19th-century character with modern interiors, a swimming pool and a three-bedroom guest cottage. The details were reported by Realtor.com.Built for a Nantucket sea captainThe house was constructed around 1834 for George C. Gardner, a sea captain and descendant of Richard Gardner, one of Nantucket’s early English settlers. Gardner made his fortune through whaling, an industry that shaped the island’s economy and identity during the 19th century. The home reflects the architectural character of that period. Its clapboard exterior features a five-bay facade, a columned portico and a widow’s walk, a rooftop platform traditionally associated with the wives of seafarers watching for ships returning from voyages.Gardner eventually shifted the original house into a carriage-house role after building a larger mansion closer to the road. The property’s story, however, was far from over.The house was moved and restoredBy the 1920s, the historic residence had fallen into disrepair. Gladys Wood later purchased it and moved the house to Main Street, where it remains today. She also hired architect Alfred Shurrocks to undertake its restoration. Shurrocks was working at the time on the restoration of the Jethro Coffin House, considered Nantucket’s oldest house.The property underwent another major revival in the early 2000s. Its owners brought in New York preservation specialist Joseph Pell Lombardi, who prepared specifications for conserving both the exterior and interior of the historic residence. That restoration was completed in 2005, after which the house was sold for $9.5 million. Its latest listing represents a substantial change in asking price, with the property now offered at $32 million.Historic details meet modern livingDespite its age, the home is designed for contemporary living. The original architectural character remains visible through features including a central hall, a turned staircase and fireplaces in the parlor, library and dining room. However, the interiors are more modern than strictly period in style. A contemporary kitchen connects with dining and sitting areas, while several living spaces provide room for entertaining.One distinctive feature is the double staircase leading from the sunroom into the garden, often referred to as “friendship stairs”. The formal dining room also pays tribute to the residence’s connection with its original sea captain owner. The main house spans more than 7,000 square feet and includes four en suite bedrooms with direct pool access. The entire third floor is dedicated to the primary suite, which includes an office and a private deck overlooking the gardens and a privately held unbuildable parcel beyond the property.Pool, guest cottage and Main Street settingThe 0.56-acre property also includes a swimming pool positioned at the rear of the lot. The pool serves both the main residence and a three-bedroom guest cottage, giving the property additional space for visitors while maintaining separation from the main living areas. Its location adds another layer to the property’s appeal. The house sits on Nantucket’s Main Street, surrounded by the island’s historic architecture, restaurants, galleries and boutiques. The water is about 10 minutes away.Nantucket’s historic district encompasses the entire island and includes more than 800 pre-Civil War buildings, making the setting particularly significant for a property whose own history stretches back nearly two centuries. The George C. Gardner House therefore arrives on the market not simply as a large luxury residence, but as a piece of Nantucket history that has been moved, restored and adapted while retaining many of the architectural details associated with its 1830s origins.Ready to Make a Smarter Property Decision? articles.title: Archaeologists found an 11th-century pendant in Russia showing a Christian saint and a Medusa-like figure
articles.summary: Rest of World News: Archaeologists have found an 11th-century pendant in Staraya Russa that combines an image of a Christian saint with a woman’s head featuring snake-lik.
articles.body: Archaeologists have found an 11th-century pendant in Staraya Russa that combines an image of a Christian saint with a woman’s head featuring snake-like hair. The copper-alloy pendant was uncovered during excavations at the Pyatnitsky site, in an ancient urban household in an area that was being developed in the 11th century. Its two sides carry different images. One features a relief of a warrior saint holding a spear and shield, identified as probably Saint Theodore Stratelates. According to Novgorod State University, the other depicts a woman’s head with snake-like hair, based on the image of Gorgon Medusa.What does the 11th-century pendant found in Staraya Russa depictThe newly found serpentine dates to the 11th century and is one of the earliest examples known from the medieval Novgorod land. It was found during excavations at the Pyatnitsky site in Staraya Russa, inside an ancient urban household. At the time, the area was still being developed. The pendant is made from a copper-based alloy. One side shows a raised image of a warrior saint holding a spear and shield, probably Theodore Stratelates. The other side shows a woman’s head with snake-like hair. Archaeologists note that this figure was likely a general representation of dark forces rather than a specific creature from ancient mythology.Christian and snake-related images shaped Serpentine pendantsSerpentine pendants were two-sided amulets, with a Christian image on one side and a snake-related image on the other. According to NovSU, the Christian side could show Jesus Christ, the Virgin Mary, the Archangel Michael, or saints linked to defeating serpents, including George the Victorious. The other side was based on the image of the Gorgon Medusa from ancient Greek mythology. These inscriptions indicate that the pendants were probably worn as protective amulets against illness. The two different images brought Christian and pagan traditions together.What the Staraya Russa pendant reveals about Byzantine connectionsThe Staraya Russa pendant adds to evidence about the community that lived in the settlement during the 11th century and its connections with other regions. Archaeologists note that the non-canonical tradition of wearing serpentine pendants came to Rus from Byzantium. The earliest such pendants found in Ancient Rus date to the 11th century, the same period as the newly discovered pendant. Along with other archaeological finds, the pendant shows that a Christian community was already present in Staraya Russa at that time. NovSU also says the finding points to well-developed cultural ties with Byzantium and the presence of local craft workshops. Before this discovery, only four serpentine pendants had been found in Staraya Russa. All four dated to the late 12th to 14th centuries.The pendant’s possible owner and place of productionArchaeologists also looked at who may have owned the pendant and where it may have been made. Sergei Toropov, director of the Novgorod State University Center for Archaeological Research, said it may have belonged to a resident of the household who was part of the broad middle social group. According to the university, poorer people could not afford such an item, while members of the elite wore jewellery made from expensive silver and gold. Researchers also indicate that the pendant may have been made using another similar object as a model. A workshop that could produce such an item may have operated in the same household where the pendant was found.Catch the latest World News and Live updates. Download the TOI app.

articles.title: A Russian immigrant lived among California’s redwoods for nearly two decades; after his death, records listed his address as a hollowed-out tree stump
articles.summary: US News: Petro Zailenko died in California in 1981, and the records that surrounded his death contained a rather unconventional detail: his occupation was list.
articles.body: Petro Zailenko died in California in 1981, and the records that surrounded his death contained a rather unconventional detail: his occupation was listed as “hermit” and his address as a hollowed-out tree stump in Hendy Woods State Park. Zailenko, known locally as the Hendy Hermit, had spent roughly 18 years living in and around the redwoods of Mendocino County, and used shelters that were made from fallen trees, bark and branches.He disappeared into the forest after working at a millCalifornia State Parks identifies Zailenko as a Russian World War II veteran who lived among the redwoods during the 1960s and 1970s. Park records say he sheltered in burned-out tree hollows, which were sometimes referred to as “goose pens,” and survived by scavenging food and using clothing that had been discarded by other people. He became known as the Hendy Hermit because of his ability to appear briefly and then disappear back into the forest.Zailenko was born in 1914 and may have arrived in the United States after leaving a Russian fishing trawler in San Francisco in the late 1950s or early 1960s, according to SFGATE's account of the park's records and local history. He eventually reached Anderson Valley, where he worked at a lumber mill, and after someone apparently asked him for immigration papers or a Social Security number, he became afraid of deportation and left for the woods.California State Parks itself notes that much of what is known about Zailenko comes from accounts by visitors, locals and park staff, which makes some commonly repeated details about his origins difficult to establish with certainty.His shelters were made from the forest around himZailenko built crude shelters from the materials around him, and SFGATE reported that he constructed watertight huts from redwood bark, branches and mats made from needles. One shelter was associated with a hollowed-out tree stump, while another became known as the Hermit Hut. He gathered food from nearby gardens and orchards and sometimes accepted food from visitors. Local accounts describe him collecting discarded clothing from campers and modifying it for himself. He also cooked over an open fire and stored food in jars and other containers.Zailenko occasionally appeared at campsites, where he was known to quietly ask visitors for matches or tobacco. Some people remembered him sitting near their fires, and others gave him food. Over time, he developed relationships with a small number of local people and park workers. California State Parks still directs visitors along the Hermit Hut Trail to the area where he once lived, and describes him as a Russian immigrant who lived alone among the trees for close to two decades.Zailenko died in 1981Zailenko's life in the woods ended in August 1981, when he became seriously ill. Local accounts say park staff found him unwell near a picnic area and arranged for him to be taken to a hospital in Ukiah. He died on August 31, 1981.An Anderson Valley Advertiser account of his history places his time in the woods at around 18 years and describes the shelters he built, including one situated in a hollowed-out redwood stump. It also records how people who encountered him remembered him as an elusive figure who knew the surrounding woods well. The state park has since expanded, and the areas associated with Zailenko are now accessible through a designated trail.Catch the latest World News and Live updates. Download the TOI app.

articles.title: ​Much of a historic Georgia town is for sale for $13.5 million; the 60-acre package includes 17 buildings, hospitality venues, residential properties, and two businesses that owners say generate about $1.26 million a year
articles.summary: US News: Interested in buying a piece of the town? Well, Georgia real estate saw a rare listing this week, with the historic town of Gay hitting the market. Ab.
articles.body: Interested in buying a piece of the town? Well, Georgia real estate saw a rare listing this week, with the historic town of Gay hitting the market. About 60 acres and 17 historic buildings spread across much of the centre of Gay, a small town, are up for sale, with an asking price of $13.5 million. The unusual listing in the Southeast includes commercial storefronts, hospitality venues, residential properties, agricultural and timber acreage, established event infrastructure, and the popular Gay Cotton Fair.Georgia’s historic town of Gay hits the marketGay sits about 50 minutes south of Atlanta. The town has largely retained its 19th-century charm, with original storefronts and historic structures still intact. The properties being sold are owned by Atlanta architect Keith Summerour and his family. His son Harrison is co-listing the offering with Bonneau Ansley, founder of Bonneau & Company, a real estate firm focused on development projects.While historic buildings often land on the market, Ansley says, this one is rare. “In more than three decades of selling real estate, I’ve never seen an opportunity quite like this. Historic buildings come to market. Farms come to market. Resorts come to market. But the chance to acquire significant ownership in an authentic American town with operating businesses, a built-in customer base and tremendous future potential is extraordinarily rare,” Bonneau Ansley said in a release.What the buyer getsThe 60-acre assemblage sits in Meriwether County, Gay, with easy access to Atlanta, Peachtree City, Senoia, Newnan, LaGrange and Columbus, as well as Hartsfield-Jackson Atlanta International Airport. The 19th-century town has almost every detail intact. The well-preserved storefronts, historic buildings and an authentic rural identity are rare to find or even recreate in today’s times. The land being sold also includes a century-old cotton gin and a former peach processing facility that once served as a shipping hub for South Georgia farms.Two businesses with recurring revenueOne of the most promising details of the sale is that it comes with two operating businesses with solid revenue streams. The Towerhouse Farm & Brewery, a craft brewery and taproom, generates approximately $510,000 annually. The package also covers the Gay Cotton Fair, a twice-yearly festival that draws roughly 60,000 visitors each time and produces about $750,000 annually. The festival is scheduled for Oct. 3–4, 2026. Combined, the two operations generate roughly $1.26 million per year, according to ownership figures provided in marketing materials.The town attracts over 100,000 visitors annually, while more than 1 million vehicles pass through Gay each year, according to the owners.Not just that, this town and surrounding areas have recently attracted attention from film and television productions seeking the cinematic appeal of west Georgia’s rolling countryside and preserved small-town settings. ‘The Walking Dead’, ‘Lawless’, ‘Till’ and ‘Barbecue Showdown’ have all filmed in West Georgia.Along with the existing operations, there are also opportunities including expanded lodging, wedding venues, corporate retreats, culinary programming, destination-driven development, conservation strategies, agricultural uses and additional brewery operations.“Gay represents something increasingly difficult to find in America: authenticity,” Keith Summerour said. “The buildings, the streets, the agricultural landscape and the stories embedded in this place were not created for tourism; they evolved naturally over generations. The opportunity is not to reinvent Gay, but to thoughtfully steward its history while helping it reach its full potential as one of the South’s most distinctive rural destinations.”This 60-acre property sits within a growing regional collection of experiential tourism and hospitality destinations, including Big Red Oak Plantation sporting preserve and Quercus, Georgia’s Relais & Châteaux hotel and dining destination.“Most real estate offerings require years of investment before meaningful revenue materialises. Gay is different. The property includes established businesses, recurring events, hospitality assets, rental income and a destination that already attracts more than 100,000 visitors each year. For the right buyer, there is an opportunity to build on an existing economic engine rather than starting from scratch,” Harrison Summerour, whose family owns and operates the properties, added.Catch the latest World News and Live updates. articles.title: In 2026, a skateboarder left Venice Beach with a damaged knee; 39 days and more than 3,000 miles later, he rolled into Florida with a new U.S. record
articles.summary: US News: Chad Caruso started his 2026 cross-country skateboard journey from Venice Beach, California, on May 1 after recovering from a re-injured knee, and thi.
articles.body: Chad Caruso started his 2026 cross-country skateboard journey from Venice Beach, California, on May 1 after recovering from a re-injured knee, and thirty-nine days later, on June 8, he arrived in Jacksonville after covering more than 3,000 miles. The journey was an attempt to improve on the Guinness World Records mark he had set in 2023, when he took 57 days, 6 hours and 56 minutes to travel from Venice Beach to Virginia Beach, Virginia. People reported that Caruso said he had re-torn his meniscus two months before the 2026 trip after previously undergoing surgery and rehabilitation.The knee injury came before the journeyCaruso had already completed one coast-to-coast skateboard trip before attempting the longer California-to-Florida route, when he travelled from Venice Beach to Virginia Beach in 2023, and covered 3,162 miles in 57 days, 6 hours and 56 minutes. Guinness World Records lists that journey as the fastest crossing of the United States on a skateboard by a male competitor. He completed it between March 24 and May 19, 2023.In 2026, Caruso planned to reach Jacksonville, Florida, on the Atlantic coast, but his preparation was interrupted by a knee problem. According to his account to WPTV, he had torn his meniscus and developed a cyst before undergoing surgery and rehabilitation, and two months before the 2026 trip, he said he re-tore the meniscus. He still started the journey from Venice Beach on May 1. People reported that the trip was funded on his credit card and that strangers along the route sometimes gave him food, water and money.He averaged about 72 miles a dayUPI reported that he travelled more than 3,000 miles between May 1 and June 8, and averaged about 72 miles a day. The route took him from Southern California across the country and into Florida, and he documented the journey online as he travelled through the different states and road conditions. Caruso was marking 10 years of sobriety and used the journey to raise money for Natural High, an organization that encourages young people to find healthy activities and avoid drugs and alcohol.Caruso has previously said that skateboarding played a role in his own recovery, and Guinness reported after his 2023 crossing that he had used long-distance skating to build his stamina during the six months before that record attempt. The 2026 journey also shortened his previous coast-to-coast time by more than 18 days, as his 2023 crossing had taken 57 days, 6 hours and 56 minutes, while the new California-to-Florida journey took 39 days.The 2026 record is still being updatedPeople and UPI reported that Caruso completed the 2026 journey in 39 days and that he had set out to break his own Guinness record. UPI described the trip as an attempt to break the record, while People reported that Caruso said he had broken it.Guinness's currently accessible record page still lists Caruso's 2023 time of 57 days, 6 hours and 56 minutes as the published record for the fastest crossing of America on a skateboard by a male competitor. Guinness also notes that records can change and are not immediately published online. That means the 39-day journey can accurately be reported as Caruso's claimed new record and a faster coast-to-coast time, while the publicly accessible Guinness listing has not yet been updated to replace the 2023 mark.Catch the latest World News and Live updates. articles.title: Turkey school shooting: 11 wounded outside Manisa high school, suspect arrested
articles.summary: Middle East News: At least 11 people were wounded after a suspected student opened fire outside a high school in Turkey's western Manisa province on Tuesday, with two o.
articles.body: At least 11 people were wounded after a suspected student opened fire outside a high school in Turkey's western Manisa province on Tuesday, with two of the injured in critical condition, officials said.The suspected shooter was arrested.The shooting took place at around 8 am local time outside Inci Uzmez Vocational and Technical Anatolian High School in the Turgutlu district, according to the local governor's office. Police and medical teams were sent to the scene.Justice minister Akin Gurlek said two chief prosecutors had been appointed to investigate the incident. The motive was not immediately known, while allegations that the student had been bullied at the school were also being investigated.Parents, grandfather detained as gun access probedAccording to Reuters, Gurlek said the suspect's mother, father and grandfather, who owned the weapon used in the attack, had been detained. He said investigators were examining how the child obtained the gun, how it had been stored and the parents' responsibilities regarding care and supervision."When the security of our children is the issue, it is not possible for any negligence, any irresponsibility to be overlooked," Gurlek said on X.Turkish media reported that the suspect was a student at the school and had taken a shotgun from his grandmother's house before opening fire near the school and attempting to flee on foot. The claim about the suspect's age was not officially confirmed.Videos show armed figure near schoolImages and videos shared online appeared to show a male figure carrying a firearm near the school before running away.Footage from outside the school also showed police keeping families and others away from the premises.The attack prompted anxious parents to rush to the school, with confrontations reported between some parents and police who were blocking access to the building.Shooting follows two deadly school attacksThe incident comes months after two school shootings in Turkey in April that left several people dead and injured. In one attack in Sanliurfa province, 16 people, mostly students, were wounded after a former student opened fire at a high school before killing himself.The following day, a 14-year-old student opened fire inside two classrooms at a school in nearby Kahramanmaras province, killing eight students and a teacher and injuring 13 others. Police killed the attacker.The April shootings prompted Turkey to introduce additional security measures at educational facilities for the 2026-27 academic year, including tighter gun controls. Security at schools had been increased at the start of the academic year last week.Vice president Cevdet Yilmaz said interior minister Mustafa Ciftci and education minister Yusuf Tekin were travelling to Manisa to conduct inspections.The education ministry also sent three national investigators to the province.Catch the latest World News and Live updates. articles.summary: US News: Iranian president Masoud Pezeshkian is set to address the United Nations General Assembly in New York this week, giving Tehran a rare opportunity to m.
articles.body: Iranian president Masoud Pezeshkian is set to address the United Nations General Assembly in New York this week, giving Tehran a rare opportunity to make its case before the international community even as Iran and the United States remain locked in a nearly seven-month-old war.But Pezeshkian and his delegation will face strict restrictions during their stay in the US. According to a report by The Wall Street Journal, they will be allowed to travel between their Manhattan hotel and the UN headquarters but cannot freely move around New York without permission.The unusual arrangement reflects the tensions surrounding Pezeshkian’s visit. The US has long imposed restrictions on Iranian diplomats, but there is little precedent for Washington hosting the leader of a country with which it is currently at war during the UN General Assembly, WSJ reported.Pezeshkian is expected to use his UN address on Wednesday to argue that Iran has been the victim of aggression and that its actions have been in self-defence, Richard Gowan, programme director for global issues and institutions at the International Crisis Group, told WSJ.The Iranian president is also seeking meetings with analysts from US and European think tanks while in New York, people familiar with the matter told WSJ. However, some analysts have expressed concerns about engaging with the Iranian delegation because of US sanctions restricting certain interactions with Tehran.US restrictions limit Iranian delegation’s movementSince 2024, the State Department has restricted the Iranian delegation’s movement largely to the route between the airport, the Millennium Hilton hotel and UN headquarters, according to WSJ. The hotel has hosted Iranian officials repeatedly since 2013.The Trump administration also introduced tighter restrictions last year, including requiring State Department permission for Iranian delegates to shop at certain stores or purchase luxury goods.The restrictions exist alongside the US obligation as host country of the UN. Under the 1947 agreement establishing the UN headquarters in New York, Washington agreed not to impose impediments on officials from member states attending UN business.Marko Milanović, a professor of international law at the University of Reading, described the situation as unusual from an optics standpoint but said the US was legally required to allow foreign dignitaries to attend the General Assembly.Iranian leaders have nevertheless used the UN as an important platform to challenge US policy for decades. In 1980, while American hostages were being held in Tehran, an Iranian delegation attended the UN and used its appearance to condemn Iraq's invasion of Iran. During the Cold War, Soviet leaders also regularly used the General Assembly to criticise Washington.Pezeshkian's appearance comes after a year of escalating confrontation. Last year, he addressed the UN months after a 12-day US-Israeli bombing campaign targeting Iran's nuclear facilities. He denied that Tehran sought nuclear weapons and accused its opponents of undermining diplomacy.This year's visit comes amid continued international tensions over Iran's nuclear programme and its disruption of shipping through the Strait of Hormuz. Iran has also faced criticism over attacks by Houthi forces in Yemen on ships in the Red Sea.US President Donald Trump, who is also scheduled to address the UN, has defended military action against Iran by accusing Tehran of being the world's leading state sponsor of terrorism and insisting that it must not develop nuclear weapons. Trump has also said he remains open to meeting Pezeshkian in New York.Despite the diplomatic activity around the General Assembly, a major breakthrough appears unlikely. UN Secretary-General António Guterres has said serious US-Iran dialogue would probably have to take place outside New York, while diplomats have indicated that no formal negotiations are currently planned during the UN week.Catch the latest World News and Live updates. articles.title: In 2020, a Miami developer bought a waterfront lot for $7.525 million and built a 9,600-square-foot family home; in 2025, he sold it for $60 million soon after moving in
articles.summary: US News: In a remarkable real estate deal, Miami developer James Curnin sold his custom-built waterfront mansion for $60 million just after moving in. This striking transaction, which showcases the soaring value of Miami's luxury properties, highlights the growing demand for newly constructed homes in prime locations.
articles.body: A Miami real-estate developer spent four years turning a waterfront lot into a custom-built family home, only to sell it for $60 million shortly after moving in. According to The Wall Street Journal, James Curnin, founder of Miami-based Clara Homes, and his wife, Jennifer Halegua, bought the roughly 0.4-acre parcel on La Gorce Island in Miami Beach for $7.525 million in 2020. They built a 9,600-square-foot residence for themselves and moved in during autumn 2024, but began receiving offers from prospective buyers soon afterwards. The property eventually sold for $60 million to Michael Arrington, founder of TechCrunch and Arrington Capital.From vacant lot to custom-built mansionIn 2020, Curnin and Halegua bought the lot on La Gorce Island, and Curnin built a house specifically designed for his family over the next four years. Construction of the house was completed in autumn 2024, and the couple moved into their new residence. This completed house has about 9,600 square feet of living space and sits directly on the waterfront. The house consists of five bedrooms along with two extra rooms for the staff. The house includes a swimming pool, lift, gym, sauna and steam room.Building rather than buying an existing mansion also shows how valuable land is in high-end property development. Research published in the Journal of Housing Economics has examined how urban land values can be separated from the value contributed by structures, showing why the underlying site can remain an important component of a property's overall worth. For Curnin, however, the house was initially intended as a family residence rather than a speculative development. That distinction would become important when buyers began approaching him almost immediately after the project was completed.A home that attracted buyers before it was listedThe property had never been marketed before the sale. Rather, as stated in The Wall Street Journal, it was when he completed the house that Curnin started getting calls from buyers about his house. The report says he was getting calls about once a week from people wanting to see the house. The interest stemmed from the rarity of newly built waterfront homes in one of Miami Beach’s prime residential areas.Later, real estate agent Jordan Karp contacted Curnin with an offer. Curnin was ready to turn it down, but he was urged to name a price that might change his mind. He named $65 million to test how serious the buyer was. The client negotiated and bought the property for $60 million.From a $7.525 million lot to a $60 million saleThe Wall Street Journal also notes that the transaction created a striking contrast between the property's original land purchase and its eventual sale price. Curnin and Halegua paid $7.525 million for the lot in 2020, while the completed home changed hands for $60 million four years later. It also reflects the cost of building the 9,600-square-foot residence and its amenities, plus the premium attached to a newly completed waterfront property in Miami Beach.For Arrington, the deal added another premium Miami property to his portfolio. Arrington bought the house after it was finished, avoiding the construction process the previous owners went through. For Curnin, the sale was harder to accept. He had planned and constructed this house specifically for his family, moving in only at the end of last year. Even though the deal yielded millions in profit, leaving this custom-made house was hard for him.The deal is an unusual example of a developer buying an empty waterfront lot, building a custom home, living there briefly and then accepting an unexpected $60 million offer. What began in 2020 as a family plan to build a home became a striking Miami Beach example of how much more a finished luxury house can be worth than the land alone.Catch the latest World News and Live updates. articles.title: A 1951 Mickey Mantle photograph used to create his famous 1952 Topps card has sold privately for $3 million, more than tripling the previous record for an unsigned sports photograph
articles.summary: US News: A rare 1951 photograph of baseball legend Mickey Mantle, which later became the basis for his iconic 1952 Topps card, has sold privately for a record .
articles.body: A rare 1951 photograph of baseball legend Mickey Mantle, which later became the basis for his iconic 1952 Topps card, has sold privately for a record $3 million. The photograph was purchased by sports memorabilia collector Ron Firman in a private treaty transaction facilitated by Hunt Auctions. The image, classified as a PSA Type I photograph, was taken just weeks before Mantle made his major-league debut with the New York Yankees. Hunt Auctions announced the sale and described the photograph as one of only a small number of known PSA Type I examples. The record transaction has drawn attention to the value of original photographs connected to historically significant sports collectibles.A photograph taken before Mantle became a starThe photograph dates to March 5, 1951, when the Yankees were holding spring training in Phoenix, Arizona. Mantle was just 19 years old and had not yet played his first major-league game. At that point, he was a highly regarded young prospect rather than the baseball icon he would eventually become. Mantle made his Yankees debut on April 17, 1951, beginning an 18-year career with the club.The photograph was taken by an unidentified photographer for the International News Service. Rather than being distributed nationally, the image was initially issued regionally for use in a local news release. That limited distribution is one reason surviving original examples are considered particularly scarce. The image later became especially important to baseball-card history when Topps used it as the visual source for Mantle's portrait on card No. 311 in its 1952 set.The photograph behind an iconic baseball cardThe 1952 Topps Mantle card is among the most recognisable pieces of postwar sports memorabilia. Although Mantle's recognised rookie card was issued by Bowman in 1951, his 1952 Topps card became one of the most coveted baseball cards in the collecting world. The newly sold photograph provides a direct connection to that famous card. Instead of being a later reproduction of Mantle, it is an original period photograph from which the card's image was created.That connection is a major part of what makes the photograph unusual. Collectors are not simply buying an early picture of Mantle; they are acquiring the original photographic source behind one of the most famous images in sports-card history.What makes it a Type I photographThe photograph carries a PSA Type I classification. In photographic collecting, a Type I image is a first-generation print developed from the original negative within approximately two years of the photograph being taken. That distinction is important because it establishes the image as a period original rather than a later copy. PSA photo authenticator Henry Yee said the $3 million sale was the highest price ever paid for a Type I photograph, including public auctions, sales and recorded private transactions.The combination of first-generation status, Mantle's historical importance and the photograph's direct connection to the 1952 Topps card has made the image particularly desirable among collectors.$3 million sets a new photography recordThe private sale significantly exceeded the previous record for an unsigned sports photograph. An original photograph connected to Mantle's 1951 Bowman rookie card had sold for $843,750 in 2024. At $3 million, the new transaction is about 3.56 times that previous mark, representing an increase of roughly 256%. It also surpassed the $1.47 million paid in 2021 for a signed photograph of baseball player Shoeless Joe Jackson, previously the record for an autographed sports photograph.The latest transaction was not conducted through a public auction. Instead, Hunt Auctions facilitated a private treaty sale, a format that can be used for exceptionally scarce collectibles whose owners and buyers prefer a private transaction. According to Yee, demand for high-end original Type I sports photographs has been increasing, while the supply of such material remains extremely limited.Collector Ron Firman acquires the rare imageThe buyer, Ron Firman, is a sports memorabilia collector who grew up in Rye, New York. He purchased the photograph through Hunt Auctions and has previously made headlines for acquiring high-value Mantle memorabilia.Firman's connection to Mantle collecting also includes the famous 1952 Topps card. A high-grade example of the card sold for $12.6 million in 2022 to an unidentified buyer from Rye. MyRye.com reported that Firman is a noted collector of vintage sports memorabilia and confirmed his purchase of the newly sold photograph. The new acquisition gives Firman an unusual piece of the history behind the iconic card: the photograph from which Mantle's famous Topps image originated.A snapshot from the beginning of Mantle's careerThe photograph ultimately represents more than a valuable piece of memorabilia. It captures Mantle at a pivotal moment, before his major-league debut and decades before he became one of baseball's most celebrated players. The Yankees star went on to become a 20-time All-Star, three-time American League MVP and seven-time World Series champion during his career.That transformation gives the 1951 photograph an unusual historical quality. It shows a teenage Mantle before the achievements that would make his name synonymous with baseball collecting. Now, more than seven decades after the photograph was taken, its connection to the 1952 Topps card has helped turn the original image into a record-setting collectible of its own.Catch the latest World News and Live updates. articles.title: In 1984, Denis Bartell crossed Australia’s Simpson Desert alone; the 390-km trek took three weeks with no backup vehicles
articles.summary: Rest of World News: In 1984, Australian explorer Denis Bartell walked 390km from west to east across the Simpson Desert in a three-week solo journey with no backup vehicl.
articles.body: In 1984, Australian explorer Denis Bartell walked 390km from west to east across the Simpson Desert in a three-week solo journey with no backup vehicles. Bartell had already crossed the desert more than 30 times in four-wheel-drive vehicles and studied the records of earlier explorers before making the journey on foot. His route took him across the desert’s red interior, where he followed the history of exploration associated with figures including John McDouall Stuart, Burke and Wills, and David Lindsay. A year later, Bartell began his 2,500km Gulf to Gulf Odyssey from Burketown to Adelaide, travelling alone across Australia and again crossing the Simpson Desert.How a man crossed Australia’s Simpson Desert alone in 1984According to Australian Geographic, Bartell’s 1984 journey as a walk “west to east across its red heart”. The account says he was interested in the history of early exploration and hoped to gain an understanding of what had driven explorers such as John McDouall Stuart and Burke and Wills to travel through Australia’s interior during the 19th century.Bartell had also studied the records of explorer David Lindsay, who crossed the Simpson in the 1880s by following a series of wells made by Indigenous people. Australian Geographic says Bartell rediscovered these wells during his own traverses of the desert. One of those wells later proved useful during his Gulf to Gulf walk after he became lost for a time.How the 390-km Simpson Desert crossing was completed soloThe Simpson Desert crossing specifically as a “3-week solo walk from west to east across the Simpson Desert 390km, no backup vehicles”. The source does not describe the journey as a 1,000km crossing, so that figure is not used here.The same account lists the Simpson Desert walk among a series of solo journeys undertaken by Bartell. His later Gulf to Gulf Odyssey involved a five-and-a-half-month walk from north to south across Australia, again passing through the centre of the Simpson Desert. That later expedition was considerably longer and included a 560km cross-country section with “no road, no tracks, compass only”.Bartell’s 2,500-km Gulf to Gulf Odyssey across AustraliaBartell’s familiarity with the Simpson Desert continued after his 1984 crossing. In 1985, he began his Gulf to Gulf Odyssey at Burketown on the Gulf of Carpentaria, travelling south towards Adelaide. He left on 7 May 1985 and reached Glenelg Jetty on 15 September after trekking 2,500km alone across Australia.A quarter of that later journey was spent crossing the Simpson Desert and its parallel dune system. Bartell already knew the desert well from his earlier 4WD crossings and his 1984 walk. His later expeditions included further solo journeys by vehicle, boat, canoe and on foot, including a two-month solo canoe journey towards Kati-Thanda/Lake Eyre.Catch the latest World News and Live updates. articles.title: In 2013, Heather Anderson hiked the Pacific Crest Trail from Mexico to Canada; 60 days and 17 hours later, she had broken the overall self-supported record.
articles.summary: US News: In 2013, Heather 'Anish' Anderson made history by hiking the Pacific Crest Trail from Mexico to Canada in an astounding 60 days, 17 hours, and 12 minutes, breaking the self-supported record and becoming the first woman to hold the overall record.
articles.body: For most hikers, crossing the Pacific Crest Trail takes months, whereas for Heather “Anish” Anderson, it became a race against the clock. In 2013, Anderson set out from the US-Mexico border with the aim of completing the 2,660-mile trail to Canada faster than anyone had done it in a self-supported style. She reached the northern terminus in 60 days, 17 hours and 12 minutes, setting the self-supported speed record at the time. The achievement was particularly notable because she became the first woman to hold the overall record, beating the previous mark by almost four days.A trail measured in thousands of milesAccording to the Pacific Crest Trail Association, the trail stretches through California, Oregon and Washington, following the mountain ranges of the western United States between the Mexican and Canadian borders. Although the route is often described as roughly 2,650 miles long, published measurements have varied slightly depending on the trail version and year. Anderson was not new to long-distance hiking when she attempted the record. She had previously completed the Pacific Crest Trail in 2005 and had also tackled the Appalachian and Continental Divide trails. Her experience gave her an understanding of the logistics involved in spending weeks in remote country, but her 2013 attempt demanded a completely different pace.She started from the southern end on June 8, 2013, and went northwards through some of the toughest areas of the trail. Rather than taking the usual five to six months that hikers take to hike the trail, Anderson took less than two months. The average that the Pacific Crest Trail Association recorded was a little over 44 miles per day. That meant hiking for long stretches each day and often continuing overnight. According to a later report, she got only five hours of sleep each day and did not take a day off during the attempt.What “self-supported” meantThe difference between a supported and a self-supported hike is key to Anderson's story. The supported hiker has a crew that supplies him or her with food, equipment and all other kinds of help during the hike. A self-supported hiker must handle all of these demands alone, carrying equipment and getting supplies during the hike. Anderson was hiking self-supported, taking care of her equipment and supplies alone. To get food or other supplies, she had to reach specific resupply points.The physical demands of long-distance hiking are considerable, especially when thousands of miles must be covered on a tight schedule. Research published in Physiological Reports examined the effects of a 112-day Pacific Crest Trail hike, documenting the physical demands of covering more than 4,000 kilometres through varied terrain and environmental conditions. The study recorded an average of 44.1 kilometres of hiking per day, along with substantial elevation gain and loss, illustrating the workload involved in sustained trail hiking. Unlike Anderson's much faster record attempt, the study followed a longer 112-day journey, providing a broader picture of the physical workload involved in hiking the trail.Even Anderson’s task proved to be shorter in time. She had to travel 44 miles every day, which meant there would be no time for prolonged rest periods during the time that she needed to reach Canada in less than 60 days. Additionally, Anderson’s route included the Sierra Nevada and the Cascade Range, meaning that besides the everyday distance, she also had to climb up and down mountains every day.60 days to the Canadian borderFollowing her start in June, Anderson travelled north and completed her trek at the Canada–United States border on August 7, 2013. It took her 60 days, 17 hours and 12 minutes, which was close to four days less than the 64-day record held by Scott Williamson since 2011. With this record, Anderson became the fastest person to complete the PCT in the self-supported category. However, Anderson's record didn't last very long as the overall fastest time for completing the PCT route. Josh Garrett managed to finish his trip the next day in 59 days, 8 hours and 14 minutes, though it was a supported journey.Her accomplishment also brought attention to how long-distance hiking records were measured. The fastest-known-time category was open to both men and women, so Anderson was competing for the overall record rather than a separate women's title. By finishing the Pacific Crest Trail faster than the previous self-supported record, she became the first woman to hold the overall self-supported record, marking a significant moment in the history of the trail.Catch the latest World News and Live updates. articles.title: In 1878, single mother Adeline Hornbek built a Colorado homestead with her children; by 1885, she owned up to 100 cattle and employed ranch hands
articles.summary: US News: In 1878, Adeline Hornbek established a homestead in Colorado’s Florissant Valley, bringing with her years of experience in frontier life, cattle work .
articles.body: In 1878, Adeline Hornbek established a homestead in Colorado’s Florissant Valley, bringing with her years of experience in frontier life, cattle work and raising a family through repeated upheaval. She was no stranger to rebuilding. By then, she had already lost husband, raised children through difficult circumstances and watched an earlier ranch destroyed by a devastating flood. The new property, set high in the valley among open meadows, aspen and pine, gave her a different opportunity. With help from her children and neighbours, she built a two-storey log house and began developing the land. Within seven years, the homestead had become a substantial cattle ranch in a community where many families depended on subsistence farming.Adeline Warfield’s life changed after the Civil War reached Indian TerritoryAdeline Warfield was born in 1833 in Franklin County, Massachusetts, an agricultural part of the state. At 17, she was living close enough to Worcester to be aware of the first National Woman’s Rights Convention, held there in 1850. Speakers encouraged women to develop their own abilities rather than accept the narrow expectations traditionally placed on them.A few years later, Warfield left Massachusetts with her brother and sister-in-law and travelled west. The move took her into the Creek Nation, in what is now Oklahoma, where her brother worked as an Indian trader. Her life there became closely tied to the trading business. She married Simon Harker, her brother’s business partner, and the couple had two children. Adeline also helped with the operation of at least two trading posts.The outbreak of the American Civil War changed the situation. Fighting and divisions spread through Indian Territory, making the area increasingly dangerous for families living and working there. Adeline, Simon and their children eventually left and moved towards Colorado, part of a wider movement of settlers heading into the rapidly developing territory.The 1864 flood that changed Adeline Warfield’s lifeThe family settled near Denver, where Adeline and Simon established a cattle ranch alongside a route used by stagecoaches travelling towards the growing settlement. Cattle and farm produce provided a market among miners, travellers and new arrivals. Adeline’s third child was born in 1863. The following year brought a disaster that altered the course of the family’s life.According to the National Park Service (NPS), In the spring of 1864, a major flash flood swept through Denver and surrounding areas. Livestock was lost, ranches were damaged and people died. The Harkers’ property was among those affected. Simon, who was already suffering from tuberculosis, became seriously ill after the flood and died several weeks later.Adeline was 31. She was left with three young children and a badly damaged ranch.How Adeline Warfield’s ranch became a family responsibility againBy this stage, Adeline had acquired practical skills that were valuable on a frontier ranch. She could ride and handle horses, understood cattle management and had already spent years working alongside her husband in the family business. She hired Elliot Hornbek, a former gold miner, to provide full-time assistance on the ranch. The two married in 1866, and Adeline later had a fourth child. The marriage eventually broke down. Elliot left, leaving Adeline once again responsible for the household and ranch.Her circumstances were difficult, but the pattern of her life was becoming clear. Rather than abandoning the property whenever conditions changed, she continued to work the land and provide for her children.Building a new ranch in Florissant ValleyIn 1876, the year Colorado entered the Union as a state, Adeline moved to the Florissant Valley. The area stood roughly 8,500 feet above sea level, with broad natural meadows and stands of aspen and pine. For cattle, the open grassland offered useful grazing. For a family establishing a homestead, however, the high-altitude setting also meant hard work and a relatively isolated way of life.Adeline began building again. With assistance from her neighbours and her teenage children, she constructed a two-storey log house containing five rooms and a separate parlour. The building became the centre of the new ranch and later survived as an important reminder of the settlement period in the valley.Hornbek also became one of the early women in the Florissant Valley and Colorado to file a homesteading claim in her own name.By 1885, the homestead had become a working ranchThe property did not remain a small family holding for long. Over the following years, Adeline expanded the ranch until it was roughly twice its original size. As reported by NPS, she eventually kept as many as 100 cattle and registered her own cattle brand. Several ranch hands were employed to help manage the operation, marking a significant change from the early days when Adeline had relied mainly on her children and neighbours.The surrounding community was developing at the same time. Many of the settlers around Florissant were practising subsistence farming, producing much of what their households needed while adapting to the conditions of a high-altitude valley.Adeline’s ranch became part of that emerging network. Her property was larger and more commercially oriented than many of the neighbouring farms, but its development was tied to the same settlement process that was bringing families into the valley.From cattle ranch to school board: Adeline helped shape FlorissantAdeline’s involvement in Florissant was not limited to cattle and land. As more homesteaders arrived, she took part in efforts to establish the basic institutions needed by the community. She helped organise the local school board, which employed a teacher and oversaw the construction of the area’s first school. Her home was also used for social gatherings, giving residents a place to meet as the settlement developed.These activities were part of the less visible work of building a frontier community. Roads, schools, farms and ranches did not develop separately. They depended on people taking responsibility for shared needs, often before formal institutions were firmly established. articles.title: India cricketers win in style as Afghan savours 'special' Games silver
articles.summary: India's dominant women retained their Asian Games cricket crown in style on Tuesday as an Afghan cyclist who once disguised herself as a man won a "special"...
articles.body:
India's dominant women retained their Asian Games cricket crown in style on Tuesday as an Afghan cyclist who once disguised herself as a man won a "special" silver.

China were streaking away in the medals table ahead of hosts Japan towards the end of the third full day of action in Aichi-Nagoya.

India won their first gold of this 20th edition of Asia's biggest sporting spectacle, with Smriti Mandhana the hero.

Her whirlwind 79 helped them crush Sri Lanka by 147 runs and win a second consecutive women's cricket title.

India smashed 216-3 off their 20 overs, the highest women's total in Games history, with 18 fours and 13 sixes.

Sri Lanka were never a threat as they were skittled for 69 in 15.4 overs and had to settle for silver.

"It's a good thing to win the first gold medal for India," opening batter Mandhana told AFP.

"It feels amazing. We've seen other athletes win gold on TV."

The men's cricket competition begins on Thursday, with India favourites to win that too.

China extended their dominance in swimming, which is taking place in Tokyo.

They have won 15 of the 20 golds in the pool so far.

But they did not have it all their own way on the night, as 17-year-old Yumeki Kojima won the 400m individual medley in an Asian Games record time of 4min 07.02sec for a Japan one-two.

Watched by Leon Marchand, the teenager now has the French superstar in his sights before the Los Angeles 2028 Olympics.

"Right now, Marchand is the highest target that I'm aiming for," said Kojima.

"I want to keep getting closer to him, even if it's little by little, and eventually surpass him."

An Afghan cyclist who disguised herself as a man to pursue her sporting dreams hopes her silver will inspire women in a country where their freedoms have been sharply curtailed.

Fariba Hashimi powered home second in the women's road race, calling the triumph "something special".

"I can't explain my feelings now," said the 23-year-old, who fled Afghanistan after Taliban authorities returned to power in 2021.

She reflected on how she was attacked with stones and trained dressed as a man when she started out in the sport as a teenager along with sister Yulduz, who is also now a pro cyclist.

"I was born inside a country where the women who dream are getting attacked, and I'm really happy that I have fought against that," said Hashimi, who is now based in Italy.

Mixed martial arts, or MMA, is making its Asian Games debut as it makes an audacious play to one day be on the Olympic stage.

One of the first champions in Games history was Teo Hui Hoon as the Singaporean clinched gold in the women's traditional -60kg class.

"I was really overwhelmed when I knew that I had won the match. I've never cried before after a fight," she said.

China top the medals table with 31 golds, with Japan a distant second on 11 and South Korea and Kazakhstan joint third with six each towards the end of Tuesday.

Games organisers meanwhile came out fighting, blaming teams for "confusion" and delays in boarding the cruise ship housing thousands of athletes.

More than 4,000 people are staying on the Costa Serena in Nagoya's port, but some had complained of long delays to get on last week.
